one_liner: Windows benchmark showing multi-threaded FILE_FLAG_NO_BUFFERING reads reach 11.3 GB/s on NVMe versus fread and memory mapping.
what_it_does: A single main.cpp harness plus two small headers (UnbufferedFile.h, MappedFile.h) that load 1,000 shuffled 1 MiB chunks of a file of at least 1 GB on Windows three ways: fopen/fread, MapViewOfFile, and CreateFileA with FILE_FLAG_NO_BUFFERING | FILE_FLAG_OVERLAPPED. It is a technique demonstration, not a library: UnbufferedFile exposes open(path), read(offset, size, target) and getPhysicalSectorSize(path), and the caller must supply sector-aligned offsets, sizes and buffers.
how_it_is_fast: Unbuffered (direct) I/O skips the Windows file cache, so data goes from the SSD by DMA straight into a sector-aligned user buffer with no extra copy and no cache bookkeeping. Throughput comes from parallelism: std::for_each(std::execution::par) runs many threads, each issuing one blocking 1 MiB overlapped ReadFile and waiting on GetOverlappedResult, which keeps enough requests in flight to approach the drive's rated 14.8 GB/s. Single-threaded, the same path reaches only 4.7-4.9 GB/s.
when_to_use: Windows apps that read large files once (point clouds, assets, model weights) and do not benefit from the OS cache.
Chunked loads of 1 MiB-scale, sector-aligned blocks that can be issued from many threads at once to saturate a PCIe 4/5 NVMe drive.
As a reference for writing your own Windows direct-I/O loader before reaching for IoRing or DirectStorage.
When memory mapping tops out (about 7 GB/s here with many threads, 1.2 GB/s with one) and you need the remaining drive bandwidth.
when_not_to_use: Linux or macOS: the code is Windows-only (MappedFile.h has a literal TODO for Linux and will not compile there); use liburing or O_DIRECT instead.
Single-threaded readers: unbuffered at one thread (4.7-4.9 GB/s) did not beat fread (4.4-6.3 GB/s) in the author's table.
Data read repeatedly or small/unaligned reads: bypassing the cache throws away reuse, and offsets, sizes and buffer addresses must be multiples of the physical sector size.
Anything you need to ship as a dependency: no LICENSE file, 2 commits, no tests, error handling is exit() with a stack trace.

integration.dependencies: Windows SDK (windows.h, winmm.lib); a C++23 standard library with <print>, <stacktrace> and parallel algorithms (MSVC)
integration.thread_safety: UnbufferedFile::read is called concurrently on one HANDLE from many threads, each with its own OVERLAPPED and event; otherwise not documented

gotchas: Harness flaw: the fread benchmarks never call fseek, so every fread reads the next sequential 1 MiB of the file instead of the shuffled range.offset; the reference-value check still passes because the same first 1,000 MiB are read in some order. fread therefore got sequential reads with OS read-ahead while the other methods read in random order, and in the 'auto' case all threads share one FILE* whose CRT lock serializes them (which explains the author's puzzle that fread par is slower than fread seq).
UnbufferedFile::read ignores the bytes-read count from GetOverlappedResult and creates and closes a Windows event per call; short reads at end of file would go unnoticed.
Cache eviction relies on an undocumented trick (open the file with FILE_FLAG_NO_BUFFERING and close it, repeated 10 times); the author confirmed it with RamMap, but it is not a supported API.

Throughput is computed with 1 GB = 10^9 bytes over 1,000 MiB actually read, and only every 1,000th byte is inspected, so the work after loading is near zero; the mapped-file numbers measure page-fault cost, not a copy into a buffer.
pick_this_over_siblings_when: Pick it when you are on Windows and want the simplest pattern for saturating NVMe; on Linux, liburing (io_uring) or SPDK are the catalogued choices, and LLFIO is the cross-platform library that wraps direct I/O properly.
verified_claims_summary: On an AMD Ryzen 9 7950X with a Samsung SSD 9100 PRO 4TB, loading 1,000 x 1 MiB chunks over 5 repetitions with the file evicted from cache, unbuffered multi-threaded reads reached 11.3-11.4 GB/s versus 6.8-7.3 GB/s for multi-threaded memory mapping and 4.2-6.3 GB/s for fread; compiler and flags are not stated (CMake project, MSVC implied). The fread rows read sequentially rather than in the shuffled order, so the comparison is not like-for-like, though the bias favors fread.
status_note: Two commits on 2026-01-22 and no LICENSE file, so all rights reserved: treat it as a reference for the technique and rewrite the roughly 100 lines you need.
